Low-latency spot currency exchange: Java matching engine, Aeron messaging, LMAX Disruptor, real-time web trading platform.

Flash Exchange — Detailed Design

Status: Draft v0.1 (design only, no implementation) · Scope: Spot trading · Date: 2026-11-03

Flash Exchange is a spot currency exchange. Registered users fund their accounts from fiat, place limit and market orders (Good-Till-Cancel by default), see a live order book, blotters and portfolio, and cancel orders. The core is a low-latency Java matching engine; all backend messaging is Aeron (IPC on-box, reliable UDP across boxes) and in-process concurrency uses the LMAX Disruptor.

Executive summary

Components (by tier: Client → Edge → Web services → Core, plus Data)

  1. Matching Engine (Java; PRIMARY + hot STANDBY) — owns order books and the authoritative trading balances (pre-trade funds hold + post-trade settlement) in one deterministic, single-writer state machine. Five internal layers: transport & sequencing → inbound Disruptor (journal ‖ replicate ‖ risk-hold → match → settle ‖ market data) → release gate & egress → in-memory state → control plane. Journal recorded in Aeron Archive (100), replicated to standby (101/102), snapshots; arbiter-driven failover with epoch fencing.
  2. Trading Service (Java) — bridge between web and engine. Authenticates sessions, validates orders (static + soft balance check), forwards SBE commands over Aeron, routes acks/execution reports to the owning user, and fans out L2 order books / trades to browsers over WebSockets (snapshot + sequenced deltas, conflated).
  3. Identity Service (Spring Boot) — registration, login, email verification, 2FA, JWT/refresh tokens, user settings (theme, colour scheme, defaults).
  4. Funding Service (Spring Boot) — fiat deposits (payment-provider adapter, mocked in phase 1), double-entry ledger, sends Deposit commands to the Matching Engine to credit trading balances.
  5. History Service (Java) — event recorder: subscribes to 2001/3001 (gaps filled from Archive replay 4001), writes orders/trades/balances history to PostgreSQL, serves history REST queries (trades blotter, order history, portfolio valuation, candles).
  6. Edge / API Gateway (Envoy or Nginx) — TLS, WAF, routing, IP rate limits, sticky WebSockets, serves the SPA.
  7. Data tier — PostgreSQL (users, ledger, history; a projection, not the source of truth) and Redis (sessions, token denylist, distributed rate limits, clOrdId idempotency, user→gateway map; never on the matching path).
  8. Web Platform (React + TypeScript SPA) — responsive trading UI: order entry, live order book with own-order highlighting, open-orders & trades blotters, portfolio, deposits, settings, dark/light themes.

Key design decisions

  • Fixed-point long prices/quantities everywhere; zero allocation on the hot path; SBE encoding; Agrona collections; object pools.
  • Single-writer per state: one matching thread per instrument shard, one risk thread per user shard; no locks on the hot path.
  • Risk inside the Matching Engine (not in Trading Service) so that funds holds and fills are serialised in one log — no double-spend races, no reconciliation loops. Trading Service still does a fast soft check for UX.
  • Determinism: time is stamped once at sequencing and journaled, never read in business logic → exact replay, hot standby and audit.
  • Release gate: no event leaves the engine until its command is journaled and acked by the standby → RPO 0.
  • Layered tiers: Client → Edge → Web services → Core, with a Data tier (PostgreSQL + Redis) kept off the hot path.
  • Market orders are IOC with a price-protection collar (default ±5% of best opposite) — never rest on the book.
  • TIF: GTC (default, preselected), IOC, FOK; GTD reserved in the schema for later.
  • Market data to browsers: L2 aggregated levels (price, total qty, order count), snapshot + sequenced incremental deltas, conflated to ≤ 20 updates/s per book per client; own-order highlighting computed client-side from the user's open orders (plus optional queue-position hint from Trading Service).

Additions to the original spec ("anything I missed")

Withdrawals; KYC/AML tiering; fee schedule (maker/taker) and fee reporting; price chart (OHLCV candles) and 24h ticker; public trade tape; self-trade prevention; post-only flag; price bands / circuit breakers and instrument halt; instrument reference data (tick size, lot size, min notional); idempotent client order IDs; cancel-all; rate limiting; 2FA, session/device management; audit log; admin/ops console (halt market, mass-cancel, user freeze); toasts/notifications for fills; CSV export of history; API keys for programmatic trading (later); reconciliation between ledger and engine balances; observability (latency histograms per hop).

Open questions for you

  1. Instruments — fiat FX pairs only (EUR/USD, GBP/USD …) or crypto too? Affects decimals and custody.
  2. Fiat deposits — real payment provider (Open Banking / Stripe / Modulr) or simulated bank for now? Design assumes a pluggable adapter, mock first.
  3. HA from day one? — design supports a single-node engine first (Archive + snapshots), then primary/standby. Aeron Cluster (Raft) remains an option if automatic quorum is preferred over an arbiter.
  4. Hosting — bare metal/VMs (best latency), or Kubernetes for non-latency-critical services only? Design assumes ME + Trading Service on tuned hosts, rest anywhere.
  5. Regulatory scope — KYC level needed before trading/deposits.

1.1 System context

1.2 Layered component view

The platform is organised in five tiers. Each tier talks only to the tier next to it or to the data tier. The one exception is the Aeron link between the web services tier and the core tier.

1.3 Deployment topology

Rules:

  • Same host → Aeron IPC. Every host runs one Aeron Media Driver. Processes on the host exchange messages through its shared-memory log buffers in /dev/shm.
  • Across hosts → Aeron reliable UDP. Use unicast for commands (1001) and replication (101/102). Use MDC (multi-destination-cast) or multicast for exec events (2001) and market data (3001), so one send from the engine reaches every gateway and service.
  • Core hosts use the Media Driver in DEDICATED threading mode with busy-spin idle strategies. Hot threads are pinned to isolated cores (isolcpus), the Archive writes to local NVMe, and A and B have a direct, low-jitter network path (same rack and switch, 10/25 GbE).
  • Arbiter / witness: a small process on a third host that watches heartbeats from both engines. It promotes the standby only when the primary is unreachable from both the witness and the standby. A monotonically increasing epoch fences off a stale primary, which prevents split-brain.
  • Gateway hosts: one Trading Service per host, or a few with separate core pinning. Scale horizontally behind the Edge with sticky WebSocket sessions.
  • Services and data hosts have no latency requirements and can run on VMs or Kubernetes.

1.5 Redis usage (kept off the hot path)

Key space Used by Purpose TTL
sess:{sessionId} Identity, Trading Service Session metadata, device, last seen refresh-token lifetime
deny:{jti} Identity, Trading Service Revoked access/refresh tokens (logout, password change) token expiry
rl:{userId}:{bucket} Trading Service, Edge Global per-user rate limits across instances, using Lua token bucket. Local buckets enforce in-process, and Redis is synced asynchronously every 100 ms 1–60 s

If Redis is unavailable, the services fall back gracefully: local rate limits only, a local idempotency cache, and the JWT signature check (the denylist check fails open only for access tokens younger than 60 s). Trading continues.

1.6 Architecture Decision Records (summary)

ADR Decision Alternatives considered Rationale
001 Primary/standby engines with a replicated journal over Aeron (101/102), arbiter-based failover with epoch fencing. Aeron Cluster (3-node Raft) kept as an upgrade path Aeron Cluster from day one; single node only Lowest and most predictable latency (one RTT to the standby), simple to reason about, matches the desired topology. Raft adds automatic quorum at the cost of an extra node and some latency
002 Trading balances and funds holds live in the Matching Engine Risk in Trading Service Holds and fills serialised in one log: no double-spend, no distributed consistency problem
003 Fixed-point long price/qty, per-instrument scale BigDecimal, double No allocation, exact
004 Engine Disruptor pipeline: journal ‖ replicate ‖ risk-hold → match → settle ‖ market data → release gate → publish Single thread Parallel durability with processing; deterministic; one writer per shard
005 Output release gate: no event leaves the engine until its command is journaled locally and acked by the standby (sync mode) Publish before durable Clients never see a fill that could be lost on failover (RPO = 0)
006 Market orders = IOC with protection collar Unbounded Prevents sweeping thin books, bounds funds hold
007 Browser market data = L2 snapshot + sequenced, conflated deltas Full book every tick Bandwidth; still full depth with per-level liquidity
008 PostgreSQL is a projection; Redis is a cache; neither is authoritative for trading state DB-first Keeps storage off the hot path; rebuildable from the journal
009 Browser protocol JSON v1, binary later Binary first Debuggability

2. Matching Engine

2.1 Goals

  • Price-time (FIFO) priority matching for spot instruments.
  • Limit orders (GTC default, IOC, FOK, post-only), market orders (IOC with price collar), cancel, cancel-all.
  • Predictable latency: engine-internal p99 ≤ 10 µs and p99.9 ≤ 50 µs, excluding the standby round trip. No GC pauses on the hot path.
  • Throughput: ≥ 1 M commands/s per engine across all instruments; ≥ 300 k/s on one hot instrument.
  • Deterministic and event-sourced: the same journal always produces the same state and outputs. This is what makes hot standby, replay and audit possible.
  • RPO = 0 for acknowledged events (release gate, §2.8). Failover RTO < 1 s.

2.2 Layered internal architecture

Layer Responsibility Threads (default core map)
L1 Transport & sequencing Poll Aeron subscription 1001, decode SBE with flyweights, assign engineSeq (monotonic) and engineTime (the primary's clock, read once per command), copy into a pre-allocated ring slot T1 ingress poller (core 2)
L2 Inbound Disruptor OrderCommand ring, 2^20 slots. Parallel consumers: Journaller (Archive, stream 100), Replicator (stream 101 to the standby, consumes acks on 102), and the business chain R1 risk → Matcher → R2 settlement, plus the market-data builder T2 journaller (core 3), T3 replicator (core 4), T4–T5 risk shards (cores 5–6), T6–T7 matcher shards (cores 7–8), T8 MD builder (core 9)
L3 Output gating & egress Release gate: hold results until the command is durable. Then SBE-encode into publications 2001 (private events) and 3001 (market data) using tryClaim T9 publisher (core 10)
L4 In-memory state Accounts (balances, holds, fee tier), order books, reference data. Each partition has exactly one writer thread —
L5 Control plane Snapshot manager, role/HA controller (epoch, heartbeats), admin commands, metrics (Agrona counters read by an exporter outside the hot path) T10 (shared, non-isolated core)

The Media Driver on the same host uses three further isolated cores: conductor, sender and receiver.

Why R1 and R2 are separate stages on the same threads. Risk state is partitioned by userId, and matching is partitioned by instrumentId. One user's hold is placed by risk shard k before matching and released or settled by the same shard k after matching. Each account balance therefore has a single writer, with no locks and no CAS. This is the same structure as LMAX and exchange-core.

2.3 Command lifecycle (NewOrder, step by step)

# Stage Action
1 Ingress poller Reads NewOrder from 1001. Rejects malformed or unsupported versions immediately with a Reject result. Claims ring sequence s, copies the fields, sets engineSeq = s, engineTime = now
2a Journaller Appends the raw command (with seq and time) to Archive publication 100. Advances journalSeq at end of batch
2b Replicator Sends the same bytes on 101. The standby acks the highest contiguous seq on 102. Sets replicatedSeq
2c R1 risk (shard userId % N) Checks user status, instrument status, static rules (tick, lot, min notional, price band) and duplicate clientOrderId (per-user open-order map). Reserves funds: BUY limit holds price × qty × (1 + takerFee) in quote; BUY market holds quoteQty or collarPx × qty × (1 + fee); SELL holds qty of base. On failure, marks the slot REJECTED(reason) and later stages skip it
3 Matcher (shard instrumentId % M) Matches against the book (§2.6). Appends MatcherEvents (TRADE, CANCEL, ACCEPT) to the slot's pre-allocated event chain. Updates level aggregates
4a R2 settlement (shard per involved user) For every TRADE, moves balances for the taker and maker, charges fees and releases price-improvement or unused holds. Each shard handles only the users it owns, so a trade between users on different shards is settled in two halves by two shards. Both halves are deterministic
4b MD builder Turns level changes into BookDelta entries and PublicTrades, keyed by bookSeq
5 Release gate Waits until s ≤ journalSeq and (sync mode) s ≤ replicatedSeq
6 Publisher Encodes OrderAccepted / ExecutionReports / BalanceUpdates on 2001 and BookDelta / PublicTrade on 3001, then frees the slot

The gate does not stall the business stages. Matching for s+1…s+k continues while s waits for the ack. Only the publisher waits, so throughput is unaffected and latency rises by one standby round trip (≈ 15–30 µs on a local 25 GbE link).

2.4 Domain model

Concept Representation
Instrument int instrumentId; base/quote currency IDs; priceScale, qtyScale, tickSize, lotSize, minQty, maxQty, minNotional, price band %, collar %, status (PRE_OPEN, TRADING, HALTED, CLOSED)
Price / quantity long fixed-point (EUR/USD price scale 5 → 1.08345 = 108345; qty scale 2)
Notional price × qty computed with Math.multiplyHigh overflow checks and rescaled to quote scale, rounding against the user for holds and exactly for fills
Order ID long, engine-assigned from a counter in state (deterministic)
Client order ID long from the client (gateway maps string → 64-bit hash plus a check), unique per user among open orders
Account userId → balances[currencyId] {available, held}, feeTier, status, openOrderCount
Side / type / TIF BUY/SELL; LIMIT/MARKET; GTC (default), IOC, FOK, GTD (reserved)
Flags POST_ONLY; STP mode (CANCEL_NEWEST default, CANCEL_OLDEST, CANCEL_BOTH, DECREMENT)

2.5 Order book

Operation Complexity How
Best bid/ask O(1) cached pointers
Add at existing level O(1) hash lookup price → level, append to tail
Add new level O(log L) tree / O(1) ladder pooled node insert, link better/worse
Cancel O(1) ordersById → unlink from FIFO → adjust aggregates → remove empty level
Match one fill O(1) head of best level
L2 snapshot depth d O(d) walk worse links

Implementation notes: price levels sit in a pooled red-black tree keyed by long, plus a Long2ObjectHashMap<price, level> for O(1) access. A dense price ladder (array indexed by (price − base)/tick) is optional for narrow-range FX instruments. Order and PriceLevel come from pre-allocated pools (sized from configuration, e.g. 10 M orders), are recycled on fill or cancel, and are never garbage-collected. Matching emits at most K events per command into the slot's fixed-size chain (K=64). A taker that would generate more is split internally into continuation slots, which keeps slot memory bounded.

2.6 Matching algorithm

match(cmd):
  book = books[cmd.instrumentId]
  opp  = cmd.side == BUY ? book.asks : book.bids
  limit = cmd.type == MARKET ? collar(book, cmd.side) : cmd.price
  if cmd.postOnly and crosses(opp.best, limit): reject(WOULD_TAKE); return
  if cmd.tif == FOK and availableQty(opp, limit) < cmd.qty: reject(FOK_NOT_FILLED); return
  remaining = cmd.qty                          // or quote budget for market BUY-by-amount
  while remaining > 0 and opp.best != null and crosses(opp.best.price, limit):
      level = opp.best
      maker = level.head
      if maker.userId == cmd.userId: applySTP(cmd, maker); continue
      q = min(remaining, maker.openQty)        // budget-limited for quote-amount market buys
      emitTrade(taker=cmd, maker, px=level.price, qty=q)   // maker price
      maker.openQty -= q; level.totalQty -= q; remaining -= q
      if maker.openQty == 0: unlink(maker); emitMakerFilled(maker); free(maker)
      if level.orderCount == 0: removeLevel(level)
  if remaining > 0:
      if cmd.type == LIMIT and cmd.tif == GTC: rest(cmd, remaining)  -> OrderAccepted(NEW|PARTIALLY_FILLED)
      else: emitCancel(cmd, remaining, IOC_REMAINDER | MARKET_NO_LIQUIDITY)

Rules:

  • Price priority, then time priority. Time is the engine sequence when the order rested, not a wall-clock time.
  • Execution price is the maker's price. Price improvement goes to the taker, and the excess hold is released in R2.
  • Collar: bestOpposite × (1 ± collar%), default 5%, fixed at the start of matching.
  • Price band (R1): reject limit orders outside ±band% of refPx (last trade, or mid if there is no trade).
  • STP is checked per maker before filling.
  • A cancel that arrives after a fill gets CancelRejected(TOO_LATE).

2.7 Risk & accounts

Event Effect (single writer: risk shard owning the user)
Deposit available[ccy] += amt (idempotent on fundingTxId, kept in a bounded dedup set and also in the snapshot)
New BUY limit available[quote] -= hold; held[quote] += hold, where hold = ceil(px × qty × (1 + takerFee))
New SELL available[base] -= qty; held[base] += qty
Fill (buyer) held[quote] -= px_exec × q × (1+fee_rate); available[base] += q; release price improvement (px_limit − px_exec) × q × (1+takerFee)
Fill (seller) held[base] -= q; available[quote] += px_exec × q × (1 − fee_rate)
Fee Credited to fee account userId=0 in the received currency
Cancel / remainder / reject after hold Release order.heldRemaining
WithdrawRequest available -= amt; pendingWithdrawal += amt → WithdrawResult finalises or reverts

Invariant (asserted in tests and by a continuous checker on the standby): for each currency, Σ(available + held + pendingWithdrawal) over all accounts, plus the fee account, equals Σ deposits − Σ withdrawals.

2.8 Durability, replication and failover

  • Replication modes (config): SYNC (default: gate waits for the standby ack, RPO 0) or ASYNC (gate waits only for the local journal, lower latency; possible loss of the last few ms on a host loss). Automatic downgrade from SYNC to ASYNC when the standby is lost, with an alert, so trading continues.
  • Determinism rules: business logic never reads the clock, randomness or environment. Only engineTime from the command is used. Collections iterate in deterministic order. The JVM, schema and code versions are identical on both nodes, and the version is checked in the replication handshake.
  • Standby outputs: the standby computes outputs but does not publish them. It may compare a hash of the outputs per batch with the primary's, via a periodic checksum on 102, to detect divergence early.
  • Epoch fencing: every 2001/3001 message carries epoch. Consumers ignore lower epochs. A demoted primary that comes back sees the higher epoch and stays passive.
  • Re-joining: a new standby loads the latest snapshot from the primary's Archive, replays the journal from the snapshot position (Archive replication), and then switches to live 101.

2.9 Snapshots and recovery

  • Taken every 5 minutes or every 1 M commands, and on admin request. The snapshot manager publishes a SnapshotBarrier command through the ring. When every stage has passed it, the state is serialised (SBE, chunked) to an Archive recording, with {snapshotSeq, journalPosition, epoch, checksum}.
  • Contents: reference data, accounts (balances, holds, fee tiers), books (orders in FIFO order per level), ID counters, deposit dedup set, bookSeq per instrument.
  • Cold recovery (both nodes lost): load the latest snapshot, replay the journal from its position, verify the checksum, then open for trading. Target < 30 s for 10 M open orders.
  • Snapshots are taken on the standby where possible, so the primary never pauses.

2.10 Commands and outputs

Inbound (1001): NewOrder, CancelOrder, CancelAll, Deposit, WithdrawRequest, WithdrawResult, RequestUserState, RequestBookSnapshot, AddUser, SetUserStatus, AddInstrument, SetInstrumentStatus, SnapshotBarrier, Heartbeat. Outbound: 2001 (OrderAccepted, OrderRejected, ExecutionReport, OrderCancelled, CancelRejected, BalanceUpdate, DepositCredited, UserState, Role), 3001 (BookDelta, PublicTrade, BookSnapshot, InstrumentStatus, Heartbeat). Details in §3.

2.11 Failure modes

Failure Detection Behaviour
Ring buffer full (burst) remainingCapacity Ingress poller stops polling, so Aeron back-pressure reaches the Trading Service, which returns BUSY to clients. Nothing is dropped silently
Publication back-pressured (slow consumer) tryClaim returns BACK_PRESSURED Publisher retries with bounded spin. MDC/multicast flow control drops the slowest receiver, which resyncs via snapshot
Standby lost No ack or heartbeat for 50 ms Downgrade to ASYNC, alert, re-join when back
Primary lost Arbiter and standby agree Promote standby, epoch + 1 (§2.8)
Archive disk full Archive error and disk metric alerts at 70% Halt new orders (instrument status HALTED); cancels still allowed
Arithmetic overflow / invariant breach Checked math, assertions Reject the command (INTERNAL), alert. Never corrupt state

2.12 Performance engineering checklist

  • -Xms = -Xmx, -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, large pages, ZGC generational. Epsilon GC for benchmarks to prove zero allocation.
  • isolcpus, nohz_full, rcu_nocbs on hot cores; IRQ affinity away from them; performance governor; deep C-states off; no SMT siblings on hot cores.
  • Aeron: ThreadingMode.DEDICATED, BusySpinIdleStrategy, term buffers in /dev/shm, socket buffers ≥ 2 MB, MTU 1408 (or jumbo 8 KB on the core link).
  • Warm-up: replay a synthetic order flow against a shadow instrument on start-up before going live (JIT).
  • Latency measured with HdrHistogram per stage. The ingress timestamp is carried in the slot. Exported every second.
  • Sizing: 1 M orders/s × ~128 B journal ≈ 128 MB/s. NVMe and the 25 GbE replication link have ample headroom.

3. Messaging & Protocol

3.1 Aeron stream and channel plan

Stream Name Producer → Consumers Same host Across hosts
1001 Commands Trading Service, Funding, Admin → Engine primary aeron:ipc aeron:udp?endpoint=core-a:40101 (unicast; after failover the clients switch to core-b)
2001 Exec events (private) Engine → Trading Services, Funding, History aeron:ipc aeron:udp?control=core-a:40201\|control-mode=dynamic (MDC: each subscriber registers, the engine sends once)
3001 Market data Engine → Trading Services, History aeron:ipc UDP multicast aeron:udp?endpoint=239.10.1.1:40301\|interface=… or MDC where multicast is unavailable (cloud)
100 Command journal Engine → local Archive (recorded) aeron:ipc —
101 Replication Primary → Standby — aeron:udp?endpoint=core-b:40111 (unicast, dedicated NIC/VLAN)
102 Replication ack + heartbeat + checksum Standby → Primary — aeron:udp?endpoint=core-a:40112
4001 Archive replay Archive → History / recovering Trading Service / re-joining standby aeron:ipc aeron:udp?endpoint=<consumer>:40401 (per replay session)
9001 Arbiter heartbeats / role commands Arbiter ↔ engines — unicast UDP

Every message on 2001 and 3001 carries engineSeq and epoch. Every message on 3001 also carries the per-instrument bookSeq.

Notes:

  • Reliable UDP: Aeron NAK-based retransmission. For MDC and multicast, use min flow control with tagged receivers so the engine is never slowed by one slow subscriber. A lagging receiver is dropped, detects the gap and resyncs (snapshot for 3001, replay 4001 or RequestUserState for 2001).
  • Term lengths: 64 MB on 3001; 16 MB on 1001, 2001 and 101. MTU 1408 (jumbo frames optional on the core link).
  • Publication API: tryClaim for messages under MTU (zero copy), offer otherwise. Back-pressure is absorbed only by the publisher stage, never by the matcher.

3.2 Message envelope (SBE)

Every message: SBE messageHeader (blockLength, templateId, schemaId, version) + common fields:

Field Type Notes
correlationId int64 set by sender, echoed in responses
ingressTimestampNs int64 latency tracing
engineSeq int64 outbound only; monotonic, gap detection & idempotent replay
engineTime int64 outbound only; primary clock captured at sequencing (journaled → deterministic)
epoch int32 outbound only; HA fencing epoch

Schema versioning: additive fields only within a major schema version; sinceVersion attributes; consumers ignore unknown templates.

3.3 Inbound commands (stream 1001 → Matching Engine)

Template (templateId) Key fields
NewOrder (1) userId, clientOrderId, instrumentId, side, orderType, timeInForce, price, quantity, quoteQuantity (market buy by amount), flags (postOnly, stpMode), expireTime (GTD, reserved)
CancelOrder (2) userId, instrumentId, orderId | clientOrderId
CancelAll (3) userId, instrumentId (0 = all)
Deposit (10) userId, currencyId, amount, fundingTxId
WithdrawRequest (11) / WithdrawResult (12) userId, currencyId, amount, fundingTxId, outcome
RequestUserState (20) userId
RequestBookSnapshot (21) instrumentId, depth
Admin: AddInstrument (30), SetInstrumentStatus (31), AddUser (32), SetUserStatus (33) —

3.4 Outbound events (Matching Engine → 2001 / 3001)

Template (templateId) Stream Key fields
OrderAccepted (101) 2001 orderId, clientOrderId, userId, instrumentId, side, type, tif, price, qty, status
OrderRejected (102) 2001 clientOrderId, rejectReason (enum: INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS, INVALID_PRICE, INVALID_QTY, BELOW_MIN_NOTIONAL, INSTRUMENT_HALTED, DUPLICATE_CLORDID, WOULD_TAKE, FOK_NOT_FILLED, OUTSIDE_PRICE_BAND, USER_SUSPENDED, UNKNOWN_ORDER)
ExecutionReport (103) 2001 (to both maker & taker) orderId, tradeId, userId, side, liquidity (MAKER/TAKER), lastPrice, lastQty, cumQty, leavesQty, avgPrice, fee, feeCcy, orderStatus
OrderCancelled (104) 2001 orderId, reason (USER, IOC_REMAINDER, STP, MARKET_NO_LIQUIDITY, ADMIN), leavesQty
CancelRejected (105) 2001 orderId, reason
BalanceUpdate (110) 2001 userId, currencyId, available, held, reason, refId
UserState (120) 2001 repeating groups: balances, open orders
BookDelta (201) 3001 instrumentId, bookSequence, repeating group {side, price, totalQty (0 = remove level), orderCount}
PublicTrade (202) 3001 instrumentId, tradeId, price, qty, aggressorSide, time
BookSnapshot (203) 3001 instrumentId, bookSequence, depth, bids[], asks[]
InstrumentStatus (204) 3001 instrumentId, status
DepositCredited (111) 2001 userId, currencyId, amount, fundingTxId
Role (130) 2001, 3001 role, epoch, primary endpoint
Heartbeat (250) 2001, 3001 engineSeq (lets consumers detect silence/gaps)

3.5 Sequencing and gap recovery

  • Aeron reliable UDP already retransmits; application-level gaps only occur after a slow-consumer disconnect or restart.
  • Private-event (2001) gaps are recovered by Archive replay (4001) from the last engineSeq, or by RequestUserState.

3.6 Browser protocol (Trading Service ↔ Web) — summary

Detailed in Trading Service §4.5. JSON over WSS v1; decimals sent as strings to avoid float rounding.

4. Trading Service

The bridge between the web platform and the Matching Engine.

4.1 Internal design

Layer Components Threads
A · Client connectivity WS/REST endpoints (JSON codec, heartbeats, back-pressure), session manager (JWT verify with cached JWKS, userId → sessions), per-session write queues Netty boss + worker event loops
B · Inbound Disruptor Validator → limits & idempotency (local token buckets, clOrdId window, soft funds check) → command encoder (SBE → 1001) 1 handler chain, pinned
C · Outbound Disruptor Aeron poller (2001 + 3001, gap and epoch checks) → user event router (acks, fills, balances; open-order and balance caches) ‖ book replicas (L2, own-order queue position) → conflator 1 poller + 1 chain, pinned
Side stores Redis (sessions, denylist, global rate limits, clOrdId keys, user→gateway map), accessed asynchronously and never awaited on the order path; PostgreSQL read once at boot for reference data —

Threads: Netty boss/worker group (I/O), 1 inbound Disruptor handler chain, 1 Aeron poller (busy-spin/backoff), 1 outbound chain (router + books), conflator timer on the event loop. Per-session write queues are bounded; a client that cannot keep up gets dropped market-data frames (conflation), never dropped private events — if the private queue overflows the session is closed and must resync.

4.2 Validation (before the engine)

Check Reject code
JWT valid, user active, KYC tier allows trading UNAUTHORIZED / FORBIDDEN
Instrument exists & TRADING INSTRUMENT_UNAVAILABLE
Price multiple of tick, qty multiple of lot, min/max qty, min notional INVALID_PRICE / INVALID_QTY / BELOW_MIN_NOTIONAL
Type/TIF combo legal (MARKET ⇒ IOC; GTC default if absent) INVALID_TIF
Price within band of last reference price (soft) OUTSIDE_PRICE_BAND
clientOrderId not seen in last 24h for user (local LRU + Redis SETNX clord:{user}:{id}) DUPLICATE_CLORDID (returns original status)
Rate limit (e.g. 50 orders/s, 500 open orders per user/instrument; local bucket, globally reconciled via Redis) RATE_LIMITED
Soft funds check using cached balances INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS (engine re-checks authoritatively)

Static validation is repeated cheaply in the engine for defence in depth, but the engine's authoritative checks are funds, duplicate orderId and instrument status.

4.3 Routing of engine events

  • Every Trading Service instance publishes commands on 1001, stamped with its gatewayId, and subscribes to 2001 (MDC). The engine sends each private event once, and every gateway receives it.
  • The user event router keeps only events for users with a session on this instance. This also covers maker fills for users connected elsewhere. At larger scale, 2001 can be partitioned into N streams by userId % N and users pinned to gateway groups by consistent hashing at the Edge.
  • Router keeps userId → Set<Session> (multiple tabs/devices) and pushes order, fill, balance messages to all of them.

4.4 Market-data fan-out

  • Maintains a full L2 replica per instrument from BookSnapshot + BookDelta.
  • On client subscribe: send snapshot (top N levels, default 50, or full) with seq, then deltas.
  • Conflation: per subscription, coalesce changed levels within a 50 ms window and send one book.delta with the latest totals per level → bounded bandwidth, browser never sees an inconsistent level.
  • Own-order highlight: client marks levels where it has open orders (from the private order feed). Optionally the server adds queueAhead per own order (sum of qty ahead in FIFO), derived from an L3 view the engine provides only to the Trading Service (not exposed publicly).
  • Public trades and 24h ticker (open/high/low/last/volume, rolled by the service) streamed on trades.<sym> and ticker.<sym>.

4.5 WebSocket API

Endpoint wss://api.flash.exchange/ws — auth via short-lived JWT in first auth message (not in URL).

Client → server

{"op":"auth","token":"<jwt>"}
{"op":"subscribe","channels":["book.EURUSD:50","trades.EURUSD","ticker.*","orders","fills","balances"]}
{"op":"unsubscribe","channels":["book.EURUSD"]}
{"op":"order.new","reqId":17,"clOrdId":"c-8f2a","symbol":"EURUSD","side":"BUY","type":"LIMIT","tif":"GTC","price":"1.08345","qty":"10000.00","postOnly":false}
{"op":"order.new","reqId":18,"clOrdId":"c-8f2b","symbol":"EURUSD","side":"BUY","type":"MARKET","quoteQty":"5000.00"}
{"op":"order.cancel","reqId":19,"orderId":"700013"}
{"op":"order.cancelAll","reqId":20,"symbol":"EURUSD"}
{"op":"ping"}

Server → client

{"ch":"book.EURUSD","type":"snapshot","seq":88112,"bids":[["1.08340","250000.00",4]],"asks":[["1.08350","120000.00",2]]}
{"ch":"book.EURUSD","type":"delta","seq":88113,"bids":[["1.08340","150000.00",3]],"asks":[]}
{"ch":"trades.EURUSD","data":[{"id":"55021","px":"1.08350","qty":"5000.00","side":"BUY","ts":1793750400123}]}
{"ch":"orders","data":{"orderId":"700013","clOrdId":"c-8f2a","status":"NEW","px":"1.08345","qty":"10000.00","filled":"0","avgPx":null,"tif":"GTC","ts":...}}
{"ch":"fills","data":{"tradeId":"55022","orderId":"700013","px":"1.08345","qty":"4000.00","liq":"MAKER","fee":"0.43","feeCcy":"USD"}}
{"ch":"balances","data":[{"ccy":"USD","available":"9567.20","held":"6500.18"}]}
{"op":"ack","reqId":17,"ok":true}
{"op":"ack","reqId":18,"ok":false,"code":"INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS","msg":"..."}

Delta semantics: [price, totalQty, orderCount]; totalQty == "0" removes the level. A client seeing seq ≠ last+1 re-subscribes.

REST (same service, for clients that prefer it): POST /api/v1/orders, DELETE /api/v1/orders/{id}, DELETE /api/v1/orders?symbol=, GET /api/v1/orders/open, GET /api/v1/balances. History endpoints live in the History Service.

4.6 Resilience

  • On start: load reference data from PostgreSQL, subscribe to 2001/3001, request book snapshots, and send RequestUserState for each user as they connect. Then go live.
  • Engine failover: on Role(PRIMARY, epoch+1) the encoder switches the 1001 destination to the new primary. Commands with no ack for 250 ms are resent with the same clientOrderId, and the engine deduplicates them. Events with an old epoch are discarded.
  • Redis outage: falls back to local rate limits and a local idempotency cache, and trading continues (see §1.5).
  • Optional cancel-on-disconnect flag per session (off by default for web users).

Responsive: ≥1280 px full grid (panels resizable, layout persisted in settings); 768–1279 px two columns; < 768 px tabbed (Chart / Book / Trade / Orders) with bottom sheet order entry.

5.3 Front-end architecture

  • WebSocket decoding and book maintenance run in a Web Worker; UI receives batched state at requestAnimationFrame cadence → smooth at high update rates.
  • Decimal arithmetic via decimal.js/big.js (never JS floats for money).
  • Blotters virtualised (react-virtuoso / TanStack Table).
  • Theming via CSS custom properties + Tailwind dark:; settings loaded at login and cached in localStorage to avoid flash of wrong theme.
  • Accessibility: WCAG 2.1 AA, keyboard navigation, colour-blind palette.
  • Security: access token in memory, refresh token in HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict cookie, CSP, no third-party scripts on trading pages.

5.4 Auth flow

6. Accounts, Funding & Data

6.1 Balance ownership

Balance view Owner Purpose
Trading balance (available, held) Matching Engine (authoritative) Funds holds and settlement on the hot path
Ledger (double-entry journal) Funding Service / PostgreSQL Money in/out of the platform, regulatory record
Balance history / portfolio History Service / PostgreSQL Projection of engine BalanceUpdate events for UI

A nightly + continuous reconciliation job checks: ledger customer liability per currency == Σ engine balances (from latest snapshot / projection). Breaks raise alerts and can freeze affected accounts.

6.2 Deposit flow (summary — full sequence in 07)

  1. User initiates deposit → Funding creates deposit(PENDING) and PSP payment intent.
  2. PSP confirms (webhook, signature verified, idempotent on PSP reference).
  3. Funding posts ledger entries DR bank_clearing / CR customer_liability:<user> and status CONFIRMED.
  4. Funding sends Deposit command (fundingTxId = idempotency key) to the Matching Engine.
  5. Engine credits available, emits BalanceUpdate → Funding marks CREDITED; Trading Service pushes balance to the user.

Phase 1 ships a Mock PSP (simulated bank with instant/delayed/failed outcomes) behind a PaymentProvider interface.

6.3 Fees

Maker/taker fee schedule per instrument and user tier (default maker 0.05%, taker 0.10%, configurable). Fees charged in the currency received, accrued to a platform fee account inside the engine, reported in ExecutionReport.

6.4 PostgreSQL schema (main tables)

Additional: candles(instrument_id, interval, open_time, o,h,l,c, volume) (TimescaleDB hypertable optional), audit_log, processed_positions(consumer, archive_position, engine_seq) for exactly-once projection, api_keys (phase 6).

Indexes: orders(user_id, status, created_at desc), fills(user_id, ts desc), fills(instrument_id, ts). Partition orders/fills monthly.

6.5 Persistence pipeline

Exactly-once effect: rows and the consumer's engine_seq are committed in one transaction; on restart replay resumes from the stored archive position and skips engine_seq ≤ stored.

6.6 History Service REST

GET /api/v1/orders?status=&symbol=&from=&to=&cursor= · GET /api/v1/fills?... · GET /api/v1/portfolio (balances + valuation from latest mid prices) · GET /api/v1/candles?symbol=&interval=&from=&to= · GET /api/v1/instruments · GET /api/v1/export/{orders|fills}.csv. Cursor-based pagination.

6.7 Redis data model

See §1.5 for the key spaces. Deployment: Redis 7 primary + replica with Sentinel (3 sentinels), AOF everysec. All keys have TTLs, and no key holds data that can't be rebuilt. Losing Redis degrades rate limiting and idempotency to per-instance and forces users to log in again, but never affects balances, orders or trades.

8. Non-functional requirements, Operations & Roadmap

8.1 Performance targets

Metric Target
Engine internal (ingress poll → egress offer) p50 ≤ 3 µs, p99 ≤ 10 µs, p99.9 ≤ 50 µs
Trading Service in → ack out (same box as engine, IPC) p99 ≤ 100 µs
Trading Service in → ack out (across network, single-node engine) p99 ≤ 250 µs (10/25 GbE, kernel bypass optional)
With SYNC replication to standby (adds one core-link RTT) p99 ≤ 150 µs same box, ≤ 300 µs across network
Browser order → ack displayed (same region) ≤ 50 ms (network dominated)
Throughput ≥ 1 M cmds/s engine; ≥ 50 k concurrent WS sessions per Trading Service instance
Market data to browser ≤ 20 updates/s per book, ≤ 100 ms staleness
Availability 99.95 % trading hours; RPO 0 (SYNC replication), RTO < 1 s failover

8.2 Security

  • TLS 1.3 everywhere external; Aeron on a private, isolated network segment (VLAN); optional Aeron transport encryption not needed inside the trusted segment.
  • Argon2id passwords; TOTP 2FA; account lockout & IP rate limiting; refresh-token rotation with reuse detection.
  • JWT RS256/EdDSA, 5-min access tokens, JWKS rotation.
  • OWASP ASVS L2 for web; CSP, CSRF protection for cookie endpoints, input validation server-side.
  • PSP webhooks: signature verification + idempotency.
  • Least-privilege DB roles; secrets in Vault/KMS; encrypted TOTP secrets.
  • Immutable audit log (who/what/when) for admin actions, logins, funding.

8.3 Observability

  • Engine: HdrHistogram per hop (ingress→risk, risk→match, match→publish), ring-buffer remaining capacity, Aeron counters (back-pressure, NAKs, retransmits, lag), snapshot duration — exported off-thread via Agrona counters → Prometheus.
  • Trading Service: sessions, msg rates, conflation drop rate, reject reasons, per-hop latency.
  • Business dashboards: orders/s, trades/s, volume per instrument, open orders, balances reconciliation status.
  • Alerts: latency SLO breach, engine failover / replication downgrade, Redis unavailable, consumer lag, reconciliation break, PSP failures.
  • Structured logs (async, off hot path) to Loki; distributed tracing on REST paths only.

8.4 Testing strategy

Level What
Unit Order book ops, matching rules, fee/hold arithmetic, validation
Property-based (jqwik) Random order streams: invariants — book never crossed, FIFO respected, conservation of funds, holds ≥ 0
Determinism Replay same log twice / on two nodes → byte-identical output
Golden-file Scenario files (commands → expected events) shared by engine and Trading Service tests
Microbenchmarks (JMH) add/cancel/match per op; allocation profiler must report 0 B/op on hot path
Latency harness Open-loop load generator with coordinated-omission-correct measurement
Integration Testcontainers (PostgreSQL, Redis) + embedded Media Driver
E2E Playwright UI tests; simulated trader bots for soak tests
Chaos Kill leader, drop packets, slow consumer, disk full on Archive

8.5 Operations

  • Environments: dev (docker-compose, single embedded driver), test, perf (tuned hardware), prod.
  • Trading sessions are 24/7 for spot; maintenance via instrument HALTED + snapshot + rolling upgrade (upgrade standby → switchover → upgrade old primary).
  • Admin actions: halt/resume instrument, mass-cancel, suspend user, adjust fee tiers — all as engine commands (audited, replayable).
  • Backups: Archive recordings replicated off-host; PostgreSQL PITR.

8.6 Delivery roadmap

Phase Deliverables Exit criteria
0 Foundations (1–2 wks) Gradle multi-module repo, SBE schemas v1 + codegen, common lib (fixed-point, ids), Media Driver configs, CI, docker-compose dev stack Schemas reviewed; build green
1 Matching Engine (4–6 wks) Order book, matching (limit/market, GTC/IOC/FOK, post-only, STP), risk holds & settlement, Disruptor pipeline, sequencer + journal (Archive), snapshots & replay, single node, admin commands, JMH + latency harness All invariants pass; p99 ≤ 10 µs on perf host; replay determinism proven
